summary: Specifies version 6 of the Internet Protocol, also called IP Next Generation or IPng. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2460.

eli5.summary: The first rulebook for the next generation of Internet addresses and packets.

subtitle: The next-generation Internet Protocol with 128-bit addresses and flexible headers.

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses were running out, and the protocol needed to support more features like mobility, security, and special services.
tldr.mechanism: IPv6 expands the address space from 32 bits to 128 bits, simplifies the main header, and introduces extension headers for optional features like routing, fragmentation, and authentication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1883 was the first specification for IPv6 (IP Next Generation). It was later superseded by RFC 2460, which is the current IPv6 standard.

today: RFC 1883 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2460, which is the current IPv6 specification. IPv6 is widely deployed today and standardized as an Internet Standard. The extensible design with optional extension headers has proven effective, allowing the protocol to evolve with new capabilities over decades.

sections.title: IPv6: The Next-Generation Internet Protocol
sections.content: IPv6 is version 6 of the Internet Protocol, designed as a successor to IPv4. The key innovation is expanding addresses from 32 bits to 128 bits, providing far more addressable nodes and supporting hierarchical addressing. Beyond addresses, IPv6 simplifies the common header by removing rarely-used IPv4 fields, adds a flow label to identify special traffic streams, and introduces extension headers for optional features, allowing new capabilities without changing the core protocol. The RFC specifies the basic IPv6 header, initially-defined extension headers, packet size handling, flow labels, priority fields, and how upper-layer protocols like TCP and UDP adapt to the longer addresses.
sections.eli5: The new Internet rulebook. Instead of 32-bit addresses (like IPv4), it uses 128-bit addresses so there are enough numbers for everything to get online. Headers are cleaner and options are more flexible.

sections.title: The IPv6 Header
sections.content: The IPv6 header is 40 bytes fixed, containing eight fields: Version (4 bits, set to 6), Priority (4 bits, marking urgency), Flow Label (24 bits, tagging related packets), Payload Length (16 bits, size of data following the header), Next Header (8 bits, type of the next header or protocol), Hop Limit (8 bits, decremented at each router and discarding the packet when zero), Source Address (128 bits), and Destination Address (128 bits). The header is significantly cleaner than IPv4: the Identification, Flags, and Fragment Offset fields are removed from the main header and moved to an optional Fragment header, reducing the common-case processing overhead.
sections.eli5: The 40-byte address label on each packet. It says who sent it, who it is for, how urgent it is, and what kind of data follows it. Much simpler than IPv4.

sections.title: Extension Headers and Options
sections.content: IPv6 moves optional features into separate extension headers that sit between the main header and the upper-layer data. The four main extension headers defined in this RFC are the Hop-by-Hop Options header (examined at every router, carrying jumbo payload information), the Routing header (specifying intermediate nodes to visit, similar to IPv4 source routing), the Fragment header (breaking large packets into smaller pieces), and the Destination Options header (carrying options examined only at the destination). A recommended ordering exists to guide implementers, though nodes must accept them in any order. Extension headers use type-length-value (TLV) encoding for options, allowing new options to be defined and handled gracefully by nodes that do not recognize them. This design is far more flexible than IPv4's fixed option fields and enables future extensions without protocol version changes.
sections.eli5: Like optional instruction cards that go with the main header. Some are read by every stop along the way (hop-by-hop), others only at the destination. If a router does not understand one, it knows how to skip it safely.

sections.title: Packet Size and Fragmentation
sections.content: IPv6 requires all links to carry packets of at least 576 octets, ensuring a minimum effective MTU. Unlike IPv4, where routers fragment oversized packets, IPv6 fragmentation is performed only by the source node. When a source discovers a link with a smaller MTU via Path MTU Discovery, it uses the Fragment header to split packets into smaller pieces. The Fragment header carries a 13-bit Fragment Offset (in 8-octet units), a 1-bit M flag (more fragments), and a 32-bit Identification value to match fragments belonging to the same original packet. The destination reassembles fragments using the source address, destination address, and identification. Reassembly has a 60-second timeout; if all fragments do not arrive within that window, the partial packet is discarded and an ICMP error is sent to the source.
sections.eli5: When a packet is too big for a link, the sender breaks it into pieces and marks each with a position number. The receiver puts them back together in the right order. If pieces do not arrive within 60 seconds, they are thrown away.

sections.title: Flow Labels and Priority
sections.content: The Flow Label field (24 bits) labels a stream of related packets from a source to a destination for which the source requests special handling, such as non-default quality of service or real-time delivery. The source assigns flow labels pseudo-randomly from 1 to 0xFFFFFF (non-zero values only; zero means no special treatment). Packets in the same flow must carry the same source address, destination address, priority, and flow label. Routers can opportunistically cache the processing state for a flow using the source address and flow label as a key, avoiding per-packet header parsing. Cached state must be discarded within 6 seconds if the flow becomes inactive. The Priority field (4 bits) identifies desired delivery priority. Values 0–7 are for congestion-controlled traffic that backs off when the network is busy (such as TCP), with recommended values like 1 for background (news), 2 for email, 4 for FTP, and 6 for interactive services. Values 8–15 are for traffic that does not back off (like real-time video or audio), where lower values indicate greater willingness to be discarded.
sections.eli5: Flow labels group packets that go together and want special treatment (like a fast lane). Priority marks which packets matter most when the network gets busy: some back off politely (like web browsing), others do not (like video calls).

sections.title: Status and Protocol Adoption
sections.content: RFC 1883 was published as a Proposed Standard in December 1995 and represents the first formal specification of IPv6 as a standards-track protocol. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 2460, which clarified and refined several aspects of the specification. IPv6 addressing is specified separately in RFC 1884 (now obsoleted by RFC 3513), and ICMPv6 (the IPv6 version of ICMP) is specified in RFC 1885 (now obsoleted by RFC 4443). The extensible design with flexible extension headers has proven robust: IPv6 continues to evolve through new extension header definitions and options without requiring core specification updates, demonstrating the foresight of this design approach.
sections.eli5: This was the first official rulebook. It was later updated to RFC 2460, which is what the Internet uses today. The design was so good that new features can still be added without breaking the basics.

fields.name: Flow Label
fields.desc: Identifies related packets requesting special handling.

fields.name: Payload Length
fields.desc: Bytes of data following this header (excluding the header itself).

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the following header: TCP, UDP, extension header, etc.

fields.name: Hop Limit
fields.desc: Decremented at each router; packet discarded when it reaches zero.
